overview.text: A familiar mouse is the house mouse, Mus musculus, a small mammal in the rodent order. It typically has brown-to-gray fur, a lighter belly, and a nearly hairless, scaled tail about as long as its head and body combined. House mice often live near people—in homes, barns, and food-storage areas—but also occur in fields and woodland. Usually active at night, they shelter in protected places and eat seeds and accessible human food. They are prey for small predators, may contaminate stored food, and are used in research because mice share important mammalian features and diseases with humans.

key_facts.text: The house mouse’s scientific name is Mus musculus; it belongs to class Mammalia and order Rodentia.
Its tail is nearly hairless and has visible scale rings; the tail is about as long as the head and body together.
House mice make nests in sheltered places near food, including hidden spots in buildings.
They are important prey for small predators, but can also consume or contaminate stored human food.
Laboratory mice help researchers study human physiology and disease; mouse models can be selectively bred or genetically engineered.
